newsitem.title: USA: FAA bomb detection training inadequate - NTSB.
newsitem.headline: FAA bomb detection training inadequate - NTSB.

text.p: The National Transportation Safety Board on Tuesday recommended new procedures for bomb-sniffing dog exercises aboard aircraft, saying current operations could inadvertently leave explosives on a scheduled flight.

The NTSB concern arose after investigators discovered minute traces of explosive chemicals in the wreckage of TWA Flight 800 that were left from a canine test conducted on the Boeing 747 six weeks before it crashed off Long Island last July 17.

During the investigation into the TWA disaster, the NTSB found that the Federal Aviation Administration dog handler worked alone rather than with a team, used "deteriorated" explosive training aids that did not have intact containers, and failed to notify anyone about the trace amounts of explosives released.
The NTSB said the handler stated he may also have spilled explosive material inside the aircraft cabin.
"Failure to report these spills led to confusion concerning the forensic evidence of explosives during examination of (TWA Flight 800) debris," the board said.

The NTSB noted the FAA had since issued new procedures and standards, but said: "The Safety Board is concerned that (they) may not be sufficient to ensure the reliability and integrity of the K-9 explosives detection program and to eliminate all opportunities for inadvertent placement of explosive materials into the system and ultimately on a scheduled flight."
The dog handler, working with the FAA's K-9 Explosives Detection Program, used the TWA Boeing 747 for a proficiency training exercise on June 10, 1996.

Based on interviews with the handler, the NTSB determined he had conducted the test without taking adequate time and precautions. In addition, the handler failed to log the removal of the explosive training aids from storage or document the identifying tail number of the aircraft used during the exercise.
"The Safety Board is concerned about such inadequate oversight controls and procedures in a safety-sensitive program that has been in place for almost 25 years," the NTSB said in a written statement.

It recommended the FAA develop and adopt new standards for the handling and placement of explosive training aids "to prevent contamination of aircraft and airport facilities" and to ensure an effective canine detection program.

"For example, dog handlers and trainers need a checklist that specifies safety-related items in the absence of which they should not conduct a training exercise on board an aircraft," the NTSB said. It also recommended working in teams, explosives record keeping, and notification and remediation procedures in the case of spills.
TWA Flight 800, bound for Paris, exploded and crashed shortly after takeoff from New York's Kennedy International Airport, killing all 230 aboard.

Investigators have not determined what caused the accident and maintain that three explanations remain viable -- a bomb, a missile or a mechanical failure. But they long ago concluded the microscopic traces of two explosives found in the wreckage were residue from the bomb-sniffing test.
The canine explosives detection program was set up in 1972 and participation has spread to more than 30 locations with a total of 100 teams.
